ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In a vacuum, there is a long, straight, thin metal wire MN, and a cylindrical metal surface of radius $R$ is placed coaxially with the wire. Assume that electrons are emitted radially and uniformly from the wire at the same speed, the mass of an electron is $m$, and the charge is $e$. Consider the interaction between emitted electrons to be negligible.

1. A constant voltage is applied only between the cylindrical surface and the wire. When the voltage is $U_{0}$, no electrons reach the cylindrical surface. Calculate the initial velocity $v_{0}$ of the emitted electrons.
2. A uniform magnetic field parallel to $MN$ is applied only within the cylindrical surface. When the magnetic flux density is $B_{0}$, electrons just barely fail to reach the cylindrical surface. Calculate the initial velocity $v_{0}$ of the electrons.
3. Remove the cylindrical surface and place a metal sheet with an arc length of $a$ and a length of $b$ at the original position of the cylindrical surface, as shown in Figure (2). The current formed by emitted electrons detected on this metal sheet is $I$, and the pressure exerted by the electron flux on this metal sheet is $p$. Determine the total kinetic energy of emitted electrons per unit length of the wire per unit time.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$\sqrt{\frac{2e U_{0}}{m}}$
$\frac{e B_{0}R}{2m}$
$\frac{\pi R e a b p^{2}}{m I}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In figure (1), a thin straight metal wire MN can be seen located on the axis of a cylindrical metal surface, and the cylinder radius is labeled R; in the middle of the cylinder, electrons are emitted uniformly from near the axis along various radial directions, and the speed is labeled v0. In figure (2), the cylindrical surface is represented by a dashed line as the original position, the axis is still MN, and a curved metal sheet is placed at a small section of the original cylindrical surface; the arc length of this metal sheet along the circumferential direction is labeled a, the length along the axial direction is labeled b, and the radius is still labeled R. Then reason: (1) When only voltage is applied, U0 plays the role of preventing electrons from reaching the cylindrical surface. In the critical case, all the initial kinetic energy of the electrons is consumed by the work done by the electric field force, so (1/2)mv0^2=eU0, obtaining v0=sqrt(2eU0/m). (2) When only a uniform magnetic field parallel to MN is applied, the initial velocity of the electrons is perpendicular to the magnetic field, and they undergo circular motion in the plane perpendicular to MN. Its cyclotron radius is rho=mv0/(eB0). When an electron starts from the axis, the maximum radial distance to the axis is the diameter of the circular motion 2rho. When it just cannot reach the cylindrical surface of radius R, 2rho=R, therefore v0=eB0R/(2m). (3) The metal sheet is located on the original cylindrical surface, the electrons radially shoot onto the metal sheet, and the area of the metal sheet is ab. The detected electron number rate is I/e. If the electrons are received by the metal sheet, then the force of the electron flow on the metal sheet equals the rate of change of momentum: pab=(I/e)mv, where v is the speed when the electrons reach the metal sheet. Therefore v=eabp/(mI). The rate of electron kinetic energy received on the metal sheet is (1/2)(I/e)mv^2. Since electrons are emitted uniformly along the circumferential direction, this metal sheet only receives the part with azimuthal-angle proportion a/(2πR) among the electrons emitted by the wire of length b; therefore the total kinetic energy emitted per unit length per unit time of the whole wire is [(1/2)(I/e)mv^2]·[2πR/(ab)]. Substituting v=eabp/(mI), the total kinetic-energy-rate density obtained is πReabp^2/(mI).
